verdict.rationale: Four converging Hebrew exclusivity formulas (phrases that close off the category of God to just one) stack across Deutero-Isaiah (the section of Isaiah from chapter 40 onward), with 'besides me' (biladey, H1107, 16 canon occurrences concentrated in Isaiah 43-45) and 'apart from me' (zulah, H2108, 13 occurrences concentrated in Isaiah 45 and Hosea 13:4) functioning as dedicated no-other-god particles (small grammar words used specifically to exclude any other god), paired with the existential negator 'there is not' (eyn, H0369) and the residue-negator 'still' or 'more' (od, H5750) over 'God' or 'gods' (elohim, H0430) and 'God' (el, H0410): Isaiah 43:10 'no god was formed' (lo notsar el), Isaiah 44:6,8 'there is no God' (eyn elohim), Isaiah 45:5,21-22 'there is none else' (eyn od), Isaiah 46:9 'there is no other God' (eyn od elohim), and Hosea 13:4 'you shall know no God apart from me' (elohim zulati lo teda) all close the divine class to YHWH (the LORD, H3068) alone in both temporal directions (past and future). Hosea 11:9 ('I am God and not man,' el anokhi velo ish) sets the creature-Creator line as a categorical foreclosure (a complete shutting down of the option) of the as-God-is-man-may-become trajectory. The Greek picks up the same pattern with 'one' (heis, G1520) governing 'God' (theos, G2316) in 1 Timothy 2:5 and James 2:19 ('God is one,' heis estin ho theos), while John 1:1-3 places the 'Word' (Logos, G3056) 'with' (pros) 'the God' (ton theon) with predicate 'God' (theos) and 'all things came into being through him' (panta di autou egeneto, ginomai G1096) marking him as the agent and not a product of becoming, Colossians 1:16-17 puts every spiritual rank ('thrones,' thronoi; 'lordships,' kyriotetes; 'rulers,' archai; 'authorities,' exousiai) on the created side of his 'creating' (ktizo, G2936), and Hebrews 1:5-8 has the Father address the Son as 'the God' (ho theos) and command angelic 'worship' (proskuneo). The pattern is pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) and unaffected by the (none-in-scope) ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants).

scripture.reasoning: The Shema (the central confession of Israel beginning 'Hear, O Israel') predicates the numeral 'one' (echad) of 'the LORD' (YHWH) our God in a verbless clause (a sentence without an explicit linking verb) (the ETCBC syntax database marks the closing element PreC, predicate complement, the noun completing the 'X is Y' statement). Whether rendered 'the LORD is one' or 'the LORD alone,' the construction asserts singular exclusivity of Israel's God, leaving no room for a plurality of true gods.

'The LORD, he is God, there is no other besides him' (YHWH hu ha-elohim, eyn od milvado) supplies the foundation formula that Isaiah 43-46 will recycle. The bare 'still, more, besides' (od, the residue-negator marker) under the existential negator 'there is not' (eyn) closes the divine class with no remainder.

The clause 'no god was formed' (lo notsar el), with the niphal (the Hebrew passive form) of 'to form' (yatsar) negated by 'not' (lo), denies that any god was ever formed before 'the LORD' (YHWH), and the following 'after me' (acharay) extends the denial forward in time. A god that comes into being, the premise of any exaltation-to-godhood scheme (a teaching that a created being can be promoted to deity), is exactly what this verse forecloses (shuts down completely) in both temporal directions (past and future).

'The LORD' (YHWH) titles himself 'first' (rishon) and 'last' (acharon) and declares 'besides me there is no God' (umibaladay eyn elohim), pairing the exclusion preposition 'besides' (biladey) with the existential negator 'there is not' (eyn) over 'God' or 'gods' (elohim). The merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) first-and-last plus the explicit no-other formula closes the divine category to one.

'Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know none' (Hayesh eloah mibaladay ve-eyn tsur bal yadati): the rhetorical question with the dedicated no-other preposition 'besides' (biladey), answered by the negated 'no Rock' (eyn tsur) plus 'the LORD's' (YHWH's) own non-knowledge, marks the lack of any other deity as 'the LORD's' (YHWH's) own attested datum (a piece of evidence God himself testifies to), not merely a confessional claim.

'I am the LORD' (Ani YHWH) followed by 'there is none else' (eyn od) and 'besides me' (zulati) repeats the exclusivity twice in one verse. The bare 'still' or 'more' (od) under the negator leaves no remainder in the divine class, ruling out additional gods of any rank.

'Am I not the LORD, and there is no other God besides me' (Halo ani YHWH ve-eyn od elohim mibaladay): three exclusivity particles stacked in a single clause, 'there is not' (eyn) plus 'still' (od) plus 'besides' (biladey), all governing 'God' or 'gods' (elohim). The grammatical density makes the foreclosure (the closing-down) of additional gods explicit, not merely implied by henotheistic preference (a worldview where one supreme god is worshipped while admitting that lesser gods exist).

'I am God and there is none else, God, and there is none like me' (Anokhi el ve-eyn od, elohim ve-efes kamoni): the cessative noun 'cessation, no more' (efes, a word denoting an end or absence) parallels 'there is none else' (eyn od) and rules out any comparable being. The grammar excludes both numerical multiplicity and ontological likeness (similarity in actual being or nature), closing both addition and similarity in the divine class.

'And apart from me you shall know no God, and there is no Savior besides me' (Elohim zulati lo teda u-moshia ayin bilti) supplies the same particle stack outside Isaiah, in 'the Twelve' (the collection of minor prophets), with 'apart from me' (zulah) and 'there is not' (ayin) combined. This is the pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) signal that the no-other-god grammar is not confined to one corpus (one collection of writings).

'For I am God and not man' (Ki el anokhi velo ish) draws the creature-Creator line as a categorical opposition between 'God' (el) and 'man' (ish) under the negator 'not' (lo). The grammar forecloses (shuts down completely) any trajectory in which the categories merge, that is, man becoming God or God being one of the men.

'The LORD is the true God, he is the living God and everlasting King' (YHWH elohim emet, hu elohim chayyim u-melek olam): 'true' (emet) and 'living' (chayyim) and 'everlasting' (olam) qualify 'God' or 'gods' (elohim) with attributes the surrounding context denies to the fabricated gods of the nations, locating reality in the one and not many.

'For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus' (Heis gar theos, heis kai mesites theou kai anthropon, anthropos Christos Iesous): the numeral 'one' (heis) governs 'God' (theos, 'one God') and then the single 'mediator' (mesites) who is 'man' (anthropos). The cardinal one matches the Hebrew 'one' (echad) and 'there is no God' (eyn-elohim) pattern, and the man-mediator clause distinguishes the human mediator from the one God rather than multiplying gods.

'You believe that God is one' (Su pisteueis hoti heis estin ho theos): the predicate 'one' (heis) with the articular (with the article 'the') 'the God' (ho theos) cites the Shema (the central confession 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one') directly into NT idiom. James commends the bare numerical confession as orthodox even of demons, marking it as the baseline monotheistic affirmation (the confession that there is only one God) across testaments.

'The God who made the world and everything in it' (Ho theos ho poiesas ton kosmon kai panta ta en autoi): the articular (with the article 'the') 'the God' (ho theos) as the unique maker of the 'world' (kosmos) and 'all things' (panta) places God on the Creator side of the line categorically, ruling out a divine being that itself came to be.

'The Word' (Logos) was 'with' (pros) 'the God' (ton theon) and 'the Word was God' (theos en ho logos): the anarthrous (without the article 'the') predicate 'God' (theos) predicates full deity of 'the Word' (Logos) while the articular (with the article 'the') 'the God' (ton theon) and the preposition 'with' or 'toward' (pros) distinguish him personally from the Father. This is one divine identity in distinct persons, not a created spiritual being ranked among others.

'All things came into being through him' (Panta di autou egeneto) and the emphatic 'not even one thing' (oude hen) that came to be apart from him place 'the Word' (Logos) as the agent through whom all things came into being. The verb 'to come to be' (ginomai) is applied to creation and explicitly not to him, marking 'the Word' (Logos) as uncreated rather than a created elder brother.

'In him all things were created' (En autoi ektisthe ta panta), with 'to create' (ktizo) governing 'all things' (ta panta) including 'thrones' (thronoi), 'lordships' (kuriotetes), 'rulers' (archai), 'authorities' (exousiai), and the summary 'through him and for him all things have been created' (di autou kai eis auton ektistai). Every created order, including the spirit ranks, is the object of his creating, which excludes him from the class of created spiritual beings.

'He is before all things' (Autos estin pro panton) and 'in him all things hold together' (ta panta en autoi synesteken). The temporal 'before' (pro) plus the present sustaining 'hold together' (synesteken) assert priority to and continuous upholding of the whole created order, a Creator role incompatible with being one created god among many.

The rhetorical 'To which of the angels did he ever say' (Tini gar eipen pote ton angelon) establishes that the Son-language ('I have begotten,' gegenneka; 'son,' huion) is never said of any angel. This severs the Son from the angelic class outright, contradicting an elder-brother-to-angels-and-Satan placement among created spirits.

When 'the firstborn' (prototokos) is brought into the world, 'let all God's angels worship him' (proskunesatosan autoi pantes angeloi theou). The angels rendering worship to the firstborn place him as the object, not a peer, of angelic worship, which is owed to God alone.

'But to the Son he says, your throne, O God, is forever and ever' (Pros de ton huion, ho thronos sou ho theos eis ton aiona tou aionos): the Father addresses the Son as 'the God' (ho theos) with an eternal 'throne' (thronos). The vocative (the direct-address form, 'O God') or predicate 'God' (theos) applied directly to the Son confirms his full deity within the one God rather than a lesser derivative divinity.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'I said you are gods' (Ani amarti elohim attem) is read by the immediately following verse 7 ('but you shall die like men,' aken ke-adam temutun) as a judicial address to human judges or rulers, a figurative use of 'gods' (elohim) for delegated authority. It does not posit additional ontological gods (gods that actually exist as divine beings in their own nature) and so does not unsettle the 'there is no God' (eyn-elohim) pattern of Isaiah 44:6 and 45:5.

Jesus citing Psalm 82 ('I said you are gods') is an a fortiori argument (a 'how-much-more' style of reasoning, from lesser to greater) from the figurative 'gods' (elohim) applied to those to whom the word of God came, not an endorsement of men becoming ontological deities (actual divine beings). The Johannine (relating to the gospel of John) context ('the Word was God,' theos en ho logos, John 1:1) keeps the term 'God' (theos) for the Son within the one divine identity, not a plurality of gods.

The anarthrous (without the article 'the') predicate 'God' (theos) in 'the Word was God' (theos en ho logos) could superficially suggest a second lesser god, but Greek predicate-nominative (a noun completing a 'X is Y' statement) word order before the verb (Colwell-type fronting, a Greek grammar pattern where a noun placed before the linking verb tends to be qualitative rather than indefinite) marks a qualitative full-deity predication (a statement of the very nature of deity), not an indefinite 'a god.' Combined with 'all things came into being through him' (panta di autou egeneto) in verse 3, 'the Word' (Logos) is uncreated deity within the one God, not an added divine being.

'Firstborn of all creation' (prototokos pases ktiseos) is glossed by the immediately following 'because' (hoti) clause: 'because in him all things were created' (hoti en autoi ektisthe ta panta). The firstborn title denotes preeminence and priority over creation, not membership in it, since he is the agent of all creating. So it does not support an elder-brother-of-creatures reading.

'Let us make man in our image' (Na'aseh adam betsalmenu): the cohortative first-person plural (a 'let us' verb form for joint action) with 'God' or 'gods' (elohim) has been read as a plurality-of-gods proof, but the parallel verbless clauses (sentences without an explicit linking verb) in Deuteronomy 6:4 and the Isaiah 43-46 'there is none else' (eyn-od) formulas govern the canon-level reading. The plural here does not predicate multiple gods on 'the LORD' (YHWH, who remains echad, one), so it does not break the no-other-god grammar.

variants.note: The bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope (not within the scope of the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) true and supplies no variant_units. The anchor verses in Hebrew (Deuteronomy 6:4, Isaiah 43:10, 44:6,8, 45:5,21-22, 46:9, Hosea 11:9, 13:4, Jeremiah 10:10) are textually stable in the Masoretic tradition (the standard Jewish manuscript tradition behind the Hebrew Old Testament), and the Greek anchors (1 Timothy 2:5, James 2:19, Acts 17:24-25, John 1:1-3, Colossians 1:16-17, Hebrews 1:5-8) carry only minor orthographic (spelling) or word-order variation in the apparatus (the variant-readings notes in critical editions) that does not touch the monotheism (one-God doctrine) or uncreated-Son claims. No CBGM data (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a manuscript-comparison method used to weigh textual variants) examined.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The Hebrew exclusivity formulas ('one,' echad; 'no god was formed,' lo notsar el; 'there is no God,' eyn elohim; 'besides,' biladey; 'apart from,' zulah; 'there is none else,' eyn od) read at face value assert one and only one God, directly excluding a plurality of true gods. The same grammar carries into Greek with 'one God' (heis theos) in 1 Timothy 2:5 and James 2:19.

A reading that treats 'God' or 'gods' (elohim) as a class admitting many true gods (with 'the LORD,' YHWH, merely supreme) cannot account for the explicit negators 'besides' (biladey), 'there is not' (eyn), 'still' (od), and 'cessation' (efes) stacked across Isaiah 43-46 and Hosea 13:4 that close the divine class to one. Strongest form: the plurals in Genesis 1:26 and the divine council of Psalm 82 indicate other 'gods' (elohim). Lexical answer: those plurals are not predicated as ontological peers (equals in actual being) in any verbless (without an explicit linking verb) 'there is none else' (eyn-od) construction, while the exclusivity particles (small grammar words that close off the category) are.

A reading on which a creature can come to be God by progression. Strongest form: Psalm 82:6 calls humans 'gods' (elohim), and 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of becoming 'partakers of divine nature' (theias koinonoi physeos). Lexical answer: Psalm 82:7 immediately qualifies them as dying like men (a judicial figurative use, where elohim names human judges acting under God's delegated authority), and the niphal (the Hebrew passive form) 'no god was formed' (lo notsar el) of Isaiah 43:10 directly negates the very category of a god that came to be, in both temporal directions (past and future). Hosea 11:9 ('I am God and not man,' el anokhi velo ish) draws the same line under 'not' (lo).

John 1:3 ('all things came into being through him,' panta di autou egeneto), Colossians 1:16-17 ('in him all things were created,' en autoi ektisthe ta panta, including 'thrones,' thronoi; 'lordships,' kuriotetes; 'rulers,' archai; 'authorities,' exousiai), and Hebrews 1:5-8 (the Son addressed as 'the God,' ho theos, and worshipped by angels) place the Son as agent and object of creation and angelic worship rather than within the created order, so the uncreated-Son clause of the stem (the propositional claim of the question being tested) holds without recourse to a created elder-brother category.

Strongest lexical form: 'God' (theos) in John 1:1 is anarthrous (without the article 'the') and could be read indefinitely ('a god'), Hebrews 1:6 has the Father bringing 'a firstborn' (prototokos) into the world (compatible with a derivative deity, a god produced from another), and Genesis 1:26 plurals indicate council. Lexical answer: the predicate-nominative (a noun completing a 'X is Y' statement) fronting (placement before the verb) in John 1:1 yields qualitative full deity, the 'firstborn' (prototokos) title is glossed by Colossians 1:16 as creator-priority not creature-status, and the Isaiah 43-46 stack of 'besides' (biladey), 'there is not' (eyn), 'still' (od), and 'cessation' (efes) forecloses (shuts down completely) any additional ontological god (a god that actually exists as a divine being in its own nature) of any rank, including spirit-children.

hermeneutics.notes: Progressive revelation (the principle that biblical truth unfolds across stages of redemptive history) is in play: the OT (Old Testament) Shema (the central confession 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one') and Isaianic monotheism (the one-God doctrine taught in Isaiah) are read forward into the NT (New Testament) 'one God' (heis theos) and the placement of the Son on the Creator side, with analogia scripturae (the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture) linking the two testaments through the shared one-God grammar.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: How many true Gods does Scripture recognize, can a human or any being come to be God, and is the Son of God presented as uncreated Creator or as a created spiritual being ranked among angels and humanity?
stem_audit.notes: The stem (the propositional claim of the question being tested) phrases 'of one substance with the Father' and 'eternal, uncreated Son' in a conciliar idiom (the formula language of historic church councils) (the 'same substance' formula, homoousios) that is a later dogmatic taxonomy (a system of doctrinal categories), not a lexical term in the cited texts. The underlying claims, one God, no exaltation to deity, and a Son who creates rather than is created, are directly testable on the lexical (word-and-grammar level) data, so the verdict is derived from the original stem while the audit notes the imported creedal vocabulary (terminology borrowed from later church creeds). The minority lens (the less-common interpretive framework on the question) (exaltation, plurality) was added with its strongest lexical form to avoid strawmanning (misrepresenting an opposing view in a weakened form).

lay_summary: Across both testaments the words used for God form a tight pattern of strict oneness. In Deuteronomy 6:4 the number 'one' (echad) is predicated of 'the LORD' (YHWH) our God, and Deuteronomy 4:35 says there is no other besides him. In Isaiah the LORD says no god was formed before me and none will be after me (43:10), there is no God besides me (44:6,8), there is none else and none besides me (45:5), no God other than me (45:21), and none like me (46:9), stacking the Hebrew exclusion particles 'besides' (biladey), 'apart from' (zulah), 'there is not' (eyn), 'still' (od), and 'cessation' (efes) that close the divine class to exactly one. Hosea 13:4 repeats the same particle stack outside Isaiah, and Hosea 11:9 draws a categorical line between God and man ('I am God and not man'), which directly forecloses any trajectory of a creature becoming God. The Greek picks this up in 1 Timothy 2:5 with 'one God' (heis theos) and one mediator the man Christ Jesus, and James 2:19 cites the Shema (the central confession of one God) as 'God is one' outright. On the Son, John 1:1-3 places 'the Word' (Logos) with God and as God and then says all things came into being through him ('came to be,' ginomai) and not one thing came to be apart from him. The verb for coming to be is applied to created things and pointedly not to the Word, so he is uncreated. Colossians 1:16-17 says all things, including thrones, dominions, rulers, and authorities, were 'created' (ktizo) in him, through him, and for him, that he is before all things, and that in him all things hold together. Hebrews 1 asks which of the angels was ever called Son, commands that all God's angels worship the firstborn, and has the Father address the Son as 'God' (theos) with an eternal throne. Together these texts place the Son on the Creator side of the line, worshipped by angels rather than ranked among them. The lexical data therefore supports the proposition that there is one and only one true God, that no being becomes God, and that the Son is uncreated rather than a created spiritual elder brother to angels or humanity. Possible counter readings from Psalm 82 and John 10:34 use the word gods figuratively for human judges (who die like men in the next verse) and do not establish additional gods.
